title: How Attachment Theory Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explain attachment theory, tracing its origins from behaviorism through John Bowlby's work on juvenile delinquency and homeless children, Mary Ainsworth's Strange Situation experiments and cross-cultural fieldwork, and the secure, avoidant, resistant/ambivalent, and disorganized attachment styles. They cover critiques and testing difficulties, Harry Harlow's monkey experiments as a cautionary example, James Robertson's hospital visitation work, implications for family separation and child welfare, adult attachment in romantic relationships, and a listener mail about the Tarot episode.

entities.name: Childcare and the Growth of Love
A Two-Year-Old Goes to the Hospital

segments.title: Opening banter and what attachment is
segments.summary: The hosts introduce attachment theory, note its pop culture presence, and define attachment as the bond between infant and caregiver, which appears universal and also occurs in other mammals and primates. They contrast it with the behaviorist view that the bond exists only to get food.

segments.title: John Bowlby and early attachment research
segments.summary: Bowlby, a British psychiatrist, argued the bond is emotional and not just about feeding. His interest is linked to his childhood nanny leaving. He studied juvenile delinquents, found home life a key factor, wrote about wartime child evacuation and family separation, and was later hired by the WHO to study homeless children. His book Childcare and the Growth of Love reached a popular audience.
topics: Childcare and the Growth of Love

segments.title: Mary Ainsworth, William Blatz, and the Strange Situation
segments.summary: Ainsworth worked with Bowlby after bringing over security theory from William Blatz. She designed the Strange Situation, a 21-minute sequence of caregiver and stranger comings and goings, and found recurring response patterns in American infants and in fieldwork in Uganda.

segments.title: Behaviorism versus attachment; Watson and parenting advice
segments.summary: Skinner's operant conditioning is contrasted with the view that attachment is innate. Behaviorist parenting advice from John B. Watson discouraged hugging and kissing children and is criticized by the hosts.

segments.title: Attachment styles: secure, avoidant, resistant, disorganized
segments.summary: The hosts describe the four infant attachment styles seen in the Strange Situation. Secure infants are distressed by separation and comforted on return. Avoidant infants appear unbothered and avoid the caregiver on return. Resistant or ambivalent infants are clingy and preoccupied. Disorganized infants show confusion and fear, often tied to caregiver trauma or inconsistency.

segments.title: Infant attachment and caregiver inconsistency
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how inconsistency and routine disruption affect infants and mention Popeye and Pappy as a playful example of attachment patterns. A brief digression covers a TikTok trend of kids faking news of parents' celebrity deaths.

segments.title: Testing attachment theory, Harry Harlow, and James Robertson
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the difficulty of testing attachment long term and the sample size and variable problems. They note cross-cultural differences, with caregiving practices varying by culture and socioeconomic status. Harry Harlow's wire and cloth monkey experiments and isolation work are described as cruel. James Robertson's hospital visitation film and the effects of family separation, including for child welfare decisions, are discussed.

segments.title: Adult attachment and romantic relationships
segments.summary: The hosts connect infant attachment styles to adult relationships, covering mentorship and romantic patterns. Anxious or ambivalent adults may be clingy, avoidant adults may value freedom and avoid intimacy, and secure adults tend to have better relationships. They note that attachment style can change with self-reflection and therapy.

segments.title: Listener mail on the Tarot episode
segments.summary: A listener criticizes the hosts' dismissive comments about tarot in an earlier episode, arguing that all belief systems are made up. The hosts respond that baseball and jello salad are different from tarot used for reflection, and sign off.
